# Testing and Code Quality {#sec-testing}

::: {.bookepigraph}

*Program testing can be used to show the presence of bugs,
but never to show their absence!*

[Edsger W. Dijkstra]{.smallcaps}, *Notes on Structured
Programming* (1972)
```{=latex}
\end{flushright}
```
:::



A function that silently sums instead of averaging will
pass every rung of the reproducibility ladder and still
be wrong on every machine that runs it. By the end of
this chapter you will be able to say, of any
computational result, whether it has merely been
reproduced or actually checked. To make that distinction
in your own analyses, the chapter develops the four
kinds of test, among them the baseline test that
@tbl-baseline-rng demonstrates on the book's own running
cohort.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Before you start

**Reading time.** About 65 minutes.

**Prerequisites.** @sec-levels, for the L0-L3 ladder and
the capture-versus-validation vocabulary this chapter
relies on throughout; @sec-compendium, for the
`inst/tinytest/` layout and the R-package archetype.
Statistically, no more than comfort reading a
coefficient table from a fitted model and a percentile
bootstrap interval; no new statistics are introduced.
R knowledge assumed: writing and calling a function,
vectors, and basic control flow.

**Objectives.** By the end of this chapter, can you:

- state the reproducibility paradox, and explain why
  reproducibility machinery cannot, by itself, detect a
  wrong answer?
- place testing in the validation register rather than
  the capture register, and say what that does and does
  not change about an analysis's position on the L0-L3
  ladder?
- write a unit test, an integration test, a
  data-validation test, and a baseline (reproducibility)
  test in `tinytest`, naming the oracle behind each?
- tell behavioral testing from implementation testing,
  and say why the second kind breaks under an honest
  refactor?
- explain why `lintr`, `styler`, and a pre-commit hook
  belong to the validation register?

**Outline.** We begin with the analyst's irreplaceable
judgments, state the paradox precisely, and treat a
pre-specified analysis plan as an oracle. We next
introduce `tinytest`'s bare-expectation style, work the
four kinds of test on the cohort and the retinopathy
trial, and separate Monte Carlo error from a change of
sampler. We then distinguish behavior from
implementation, treat linting, styling, and the
pre-commit gate, and set out what 'validation' means in
regulated work, before turning to how one analyst reviews
another's code. The later sections show how the
emphasis shifts across archetypes, give a worked
example of the paradox itself, discuss collaborating
with an LLM, and apply all four kinds of test to the
running cohort. The chapter closes with exercises, a
cheat sheet, and further reading.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: from earlier chapters

Three failures reach you in one week. (a) A collaborator
runs a project that has no `renv.lock`, installs newer
versions of its packages than the author used, and a
summary table changes. (b) A colleague's `renv::restore()`
of a complete lockfile stops because a spatial package
cannot find GDAL. (c) A figure still shows last month's
counts after the raw extract was corrected, although the
report rendered without error. For each, name the
determinant layer that failed and the earlier chapter's
remedy.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Of the three failures in this warm-up, (a) is the
package-version layer. With no lockfile the project has
not reached L1, and the remedy is the L1 step of
@sec-dependencies: a lockfile written by
`renv::snapshot()` and read by `renv::restore()`. (b) is
the operating-system and system-library layer. A
lockfile pins the R packages and nothing beneath them,
and GDAL is not an R package. The remedy is the container
of @sec-containers, which reaches L2 only with a
digest-pinned base, a dated snapshot, and the lockfile
restored inside it. (c) is a stale derived file, not an
environment layer at all: the correction never reached
the figure. The remedy is a pipeline in which the raw
extract is a `format = 'file'` target, so that `targets`
rebuilds everything downstream of it (@sec-pipelines).
:::
:::

## Where this sits on the stack

Testing is this book's clearest case of pure
validation. It is also, among the chapters so far, one
that captures nothing at all. That is, a test suite adds
no package to the lockfile and no layer to the image.
@fig-stack-testing marks that asymmetry on the shared
determinant stack. The two layers this chapter writes
code against, the analysis code and the input data, are
validated here, not captured. The surrounding chapters
captured them already, and this chapter only confirms
they still behave.

```{.r .cell-code}
  title = 'Testing validates code and data; it captures neither')
```

## Orientation

Consider a registry study in which an analyst
has written a small function to compute a mean
biomarker value for each treatment arm. The
function carries a simple bug: it sums the values
but forgets to divide by their count. The
analysis runs without error. It produces a
table, a figure, a p-value. Sent to a colleague,
cloned onto a second machine, restored from a
lockfile inside a pinned container, it runs again
and produces the identical table, the identical
figure, the identical p-value. Every rung of the
ladder of @sec-levels is satisfied: the source is
locatable, the packages are pinned, the
environment is pinned. The result is perfectly
reproducible, and it is wrong.

This is the reproducibility paradox, and it is
the pivot of this chapter. A buggy function that
returns the wrong answer returns the *same* wrong
answer everywhere, on every machine, at every
later date. Reproducibility machinery, faithfully
applied, does not detect the error; it propagates
it with mechanical fidelity. The lesson, pressed
by Leek and Peng in their aptly titled note that
reproducible research can still be wrong
[@leek2015], is that reproducibility is a floor
and not a ceiling. It guarantees that a result can
be regenerated. It says nothing whatever about
whether the result is correct.

The remedy is testing. But why does testing belong
in a book about reproducibility, rather than in a
separate book about software engineering? The
reason is precisely the paradox. Pinning a
package version, building a container, restoring a
lockfile: each of these *captures* a determinant
of the computation, and none of them examines
whether the computation is right. Testing captures
nothing. A test adds no package to the lockfile
and no library to the image. What a test does is
*confirm* that a function, a pipeline, or a dataset
behaves as the analyst intended. It belongs, in the
vocabulary this book has used since @sec-intro, to
the validation register rather than the capture
register, alongside the continuous integration and
output verification of @sec-verification. Capture
fixes the inputs; validation checks that the
fixed inputs still produce the answer they are
supposed to. A reproducible analysis without tests
is trusted; a reproducible analysis with tests is
checked.

There is a further and more constructive link to
the ladder. The highest rung, L3 verified, is
reached not by capturing more but by *confirming*
that a recorded computational output regenerates.
That confirmation is itself a test, of a
particular kind we shall meet below as the
baseline test, so the topmost level is defined
by a test.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: the paradox

A colleague reports that their analysis reaches L2
pinned environment and argues this means the reported
hazard ratio must be correct. What is wrong with the
argument?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

L2 is a claim about capture, that the packages and the
environment are pinned so the same code produces the
same output everywhere. It is not a claim about
correctness: a pinned, containerized analysis still
reproduces a wrong hazard ratio exactly, if the code
that computes it is wrong. Only a test, comparing
against an independent oracle, bears on whether the
number is right.
:::
:::

## The analyst's contribution

Testing tooling runs the checks, tallies the
passes and failures, and reports them. It does not
originate any of the judgments that give a test
its value. Three of them underlie everything that
follows.

1. **The analyst decides what 'correct' means.**
   A test compares a computed value against an
   expected one, and the expected one has to come
   from somewhere outside the code under test. This
   source of independent truth is called an oracle.
   Examples are a mean of one, two, and three that the
   analyst knows to be two; a count of rows that a data
   dictionary fixes at some known number; a
   coefficient that a textbook formula supplies. No
   tool knows the right answer. The analyst supplies
   it, and a test is only as trustworthy as the
   oracle behind it.

2. **The analyst chooses which behaviors to pin.**
   A function has an infinity of properties, most of
   them incidental to its purpose. The analyst
   decides which few constitute the function's
   contract, the behaviors a future change must not
   break, and writes tests for those. This is the
   distinction, developed below, between testing
   behavior and testing implementation.

3. **The analyst encodes the domain constraints.**
   Consider the rules that an age lies between zero
   and one hundred and twenty, that a treatment arm is
   one of a fixed set of labels, and that a
   probability sits in the unit interval. These are
   not facts the computer can infer. They are clinical
   and scientific knowledge. A data-validation test is
   the place where that knowledge is written down in
   executable form, so that a violation halts the
   analysis rather than passing silently into a
   result.

::: {.callout-note}
## The vocabulary of this chapter

- **Unit test.** A focused check that one small
  piece of code, typically a single function,
  behaves as intended on known inputs.
- **Integration test.** A check that several
  components behave correctly when composed into a
  pipeline, from raw input to final result.
- **Data-validation test.** A check on the data
  itself, not the code: that a value lies in
  a plausible range, that no impossible ages appear,
  that the expected columns are present.
- **Reproducibility test.** A check that a recorded
  computational result regenerates. The form that can
  fail is the *baseline test*, which compares a fresh
  result with a value recorded in an earlier session
  and committed, within a stated tolerance. Two runs
  in one session do not qualify.
- **Oracle.** The source of independent truth a
  test compares against; the known correct answer.
- **`tinytest`.** A lightweight, zero-dependency R
  testing framework in which a test file is a plain
  script of bare, top-level expectation calls
  [@vanderloo2020].
- **Expectation.** A single assertion, such as
  `expect_equal(actual, expected)`, that passes or
  fails.
- **Linting.** Static analysis of source code for
  stylistic and likely-error patterns, performed by
  `lintr`, without running the code.
- **Styling.** Automatic reformatting of source code
  to a consistent layout, performed by `styler`.
- **Pre-commit hook.** A script that git runs
  automatically before a commit is recorded, used
  here to run the linter and the styler as a gate.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: three judgments

Name the three judgments that a testing tool cannot
make on its own, and that fall to the analyst instead.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The first is what 'correct' means for a given input,
supplied by an oracle outside the code under test. The
second is which behaviors of a function constitute its
contract and so deserve a test. The third is which
domain constraints, such as a plausible age range, the
data itself must satisfy.
:::
:::

## The reproducibility paradox, stated precisely

A computational result depends on the code, the
data, and the stack of determinants beneath them
that @sec-levels enumerated. The capture tools of
Part II fix those determinants, so that the
mapping from input to output is held constant
across machines and across time. But holding a
mapping constant says nothing about whether the
mapping is the intended one. If the code encodes
the function 'sum' where the analyst meant the
function 'mean', then capture faithfully preserves
'sum', and every reproduction returns the sum. The
error is not in the reproduction; the reproduction
is flawless. The error is in the mapping, and the
only instrument that examines the mapping is a
test.

Two consequences follow, and they cut in opposite
directions. On the one hand, a result that fails to
reproduce is thereby shown to be untrustworthy,
which is a genuine service; irreproducibility is a
detectable defect. On the other hand, a result that
does reproduce has been shown only to be stable, not
to be right. Stability is easily mistaken for
correctness by an analyst who has watched the same
number appear three times. Testing exists to break
the false inference from 'it came out the same' to
'it came out correct'.

::: {.callout-important}
## The honest level

This chapter's own practice reaches a baseline test
on one bootstrap bound (@tbl-baseline-rng) and a short,
illustrative suite of unit, integration, and
data-validation checks on hand-picked examples. It
establishes that those particular results regenerate
and that those particular functions behave as
intended. It says nothing whatsoever about any
function, dataset, or computation this chapter did not
choose to test.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: capture, faithfully

If the code encodes 'sum' where the analyst meant
'mean', what does capturing the environment do to that
error, and what does it not do?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Capture preserves the error exactly: every reproduction
on every pinned machine returns the same sum, forever.
It does nothing to detect the error, because capture
examines only whether the mapping from input to output
is held constant, never whether the mapping is the
intended one. Only a test, comparing against an
independent oracle, examines the mapping itself.
:::
:::

## The analysis plan as an oracle

The oracle introduced above sits at the level of a
single function: a hand-computed mean, a row count a
data dictionary fixes. The same structure scales up to
the level of the whole analysis's primary result, and
doing so closes a gap the paradox otherwise leaves
open.

A **pre-specified analysis plan** states in advance the
primary endpoint, the model, the covariates, and the
comparison that will answer the study's main question.
It is also called a statistical analysis plan, or, when
it is registered publicly before the data are seen, a
pre-registration. Written and dated before the analyst
has looked at the outcome data, it is computed
independently of any code's output in exactly the sense
the Vocabulary box above requires of an oracle. That is,
it specifies what the correct analysis looks like, not
by running anything, but by committing in writing to a
choice that the data cannot later be allowed to revise.

A function-level oracle, such as the hand-computed mean
described above, catches a coding error: the function
returns the wrong number for a known input. It says
nothing about whether the analysis itself asks the right
question. Consider an analysis built by trying several
models, several covariate sets, or several endpoints and
reporting the one that reached significance. It can be
bug-free in every function and pass every unit test. It
can also still reproduce exactly on a second machine,
because reproduction only checks that the same code
returns the same output. The reproducibility paradox
stated above applies again, one level up. A fully
reproducible analysis can still be the wrong analysis,
chosen with the benefit of having already seen the
answer. A pre-specified plan is the oracle that
guards against this failure, because it fixes the
intended analysis before the data could have shaped it.

The two oracles differ in what independence they supply.
A function's oracle is independent of the code that
computes the value; a pre-specified plan is independent
of the data that will later be analyzed. Both are
necessary, and neither substitutes for the other. A
bug-free implementation of an unregistered, data-driven
analysis is still untrustworthy in the way the plan would
have prevented. Conversely, a faithful implementation of a
pre-specified plan can still contain a coding error that
only a function-level oracle would catch.

In a research compendium, a pre-specified plan is a
dated document, committed to the repository (or
deposited externally, as on the Open Science Framework)
before the raw data arrive, or before they are
unblinded. Checking an analysis against it is not an
`expect_equal()` call but a review step: do the fitted
model's formula, the stated primary comparison, and the
decision rule actually implemented match what the plan
specified? Where the match can be stated mechanically,
for example that `fit_model()` fits the formula the plan
names, a test can assert it directly. Such a test
compares the model's formula (as text, or as a parsed
call) against a
string recorded from the plan rather than against
anything the analysis itself computed.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: two oracles

A colleague's bootstrap confidence interval regenerates
bit for bit on a second machine, and every unit test in
the package passes. Is this enough to trust the
reported result as the study's primary finding? What
additional check, and what additional oracle, would you
ask for?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

No. Reproducing exactly and passing every unit test
shows that the code is a faithful, bug-free
implementation of whatever analysis it runs. Neither
check examines whether that analysis is the one the
study committed to before seeing the data. The
additional check is whether the fitted model, the
endpoint, and the comparison match a pre-specified
analysis plan dated before the data arrived. That plan
is the oracle: a source of what the correct analysis
should look like, supplied independently of any result
the code could produce.
:::
:::

## tinytest: bare expectations

The framework this book uses adopts `tinytest`
[@vanderloo2020] as its testing tool. The choice
rewards a moment's explanation because it shapes how
the tests look. `tinytest` is lightweight and carries
no dependencies of its own, which matters in a
reproducible compendium. Every additional test
dependency enlarges the lockfile and the container
image, and a testing framework that dragged in a
dozen packages would tax the very machinery it is
meant to protect. The more visible
consequence is stylistic. A `tinytest` test file is
an ordinary R script containing bare, top-level
expectation calls, with no wrapping function around
them.

A reader who has met `testthat` will notice the
difference at once. Where `testthat` nests each
assertion inside a `test_that('description', {
... })` block, `tinytest` writes the assertion
directly:

```r
# inst/tinytest/test-calculate_mean.R
expect_equal(calculate_mean(c(1, 2, 3)), 2)
expect_equal(calculate_mean(5), 5)
expect_true(is.nan(calculate_mean(numeric(0))))
```

Each line is a complete test. The file is also a
runnable script, so during development an analyst
can source it directly and watch the expectations
evaluate. The available expectations cover the
common cases (`expect_equal()`, `expect_true()`,
`expect_false()`, `expect_identical()`,
`expect_error()`, `expect_inherits()`, and a few
others). A compendium's tests are collected in
`inst/tinytest/` and driven by a small
`tests/tinytest.R` runner that `R CMD check`
invokes. `tinytest` runs each file with the test
directory as its working directory. A test that
reads a project file from the root therefore reaches
it through `../../`, as the listings below do. We
follow the convention throughout: bare top-level
expectations, one concern per file, named
`test-<thing>.R`.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: reading a bare file

A `tinytest` test file contains no `test_that()` call
and no function definition around its expectations.
What does that tell you about how to run one line of
it during development?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Because each expectation is a bare, top-level
statement, the file is an ordinary runnable R script.
An analyst can `source()` the whole file, or send a
single line to the console, and watch that one
expectation evaluate immediately, with no need to
locate it inside a nested block first.
:::
:::

## The four kinds of test

A research compendium wants four kinds of test, and
they form a progression from the smallest unit of
code to the reproduction of a whole result. We take
them in turn, illustrating each on synthetic data
of the sort a health study might produce.

### Unit tests of functions

A unit test checks that one function behaves as
intended on inputs whose correct outputs are known
independently. The mean function of the orientation,
here called `calculate_mean`, is the canonical case.
Its contract is
that it returns the arithmetic mean, and the oracle
is arithmetic done by hand:

```r
# inst/tinytest/test-calculate_mean.R
expect_equal(calculate_mean(c(2, 4, 6)), 4)
expect_equal(calculate_mean(c(-1, 0, 1)), 0)
expect_true(is.nan(calculate_mean(numeric(0))))
expect_equal(calculate_mean(c(1, NA, 3),
                            na.rm = TRUE), 2)
```

The first two lines pin the ordinary behavior
against hand-computed answers. The third and fourth
pin the edge cases, the empty vector and the
missing value, which are exactly the inputs on which
an untested function tends to misbehave. A unit test
suite is, in effect, a written record of what the
analyst believes each function promises.

### Integration tests of the pipeline

A unit test exercises a function in isolation, but a
health analysis is rarely one function. It is a
pipeline, in which raw data is loaded, cleaned,
modeled, and summarized, and the components can be
individually correct yet compose incorrectly. An
integration test runs the pipeline end to end and
checks the result:

```r
# abridged from inst/tinytest/test-cohort.R
raw <- load_cohort('../../analysis/data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv')
cohort <- clean_cohort(raw)
fit <- fit_model(cohort)
summary_tbl <- summarise_fit(fit)

expect_true(is.numeric(coef(fit)))
expect_true(all(c('term', 'estimate') %in%
                names(summary_tbl)))
expect_equal(nrow(summary_tbl), 3L)
```

The first expectation tests the contract that
`coef(fit)` returns numeric coefficients, which is
what `summarise_fit()` needs to proceed. Testing
`expect_inherits(fit, 'lm')` would also pass here,
because `glm` inherits from `lm`, but it would break
the moment the function was upgraded to `fit_cox()`
returning a `coxph`, which does not. Testing the
interface ('does `coef()` return numeric values?')
survives that migration; testing the class does not.
The book's own compendium does not perform this
migration: `fit_cox()` was added beside `fit_model()`
rather than replacing it, and its tests sit in a file
of their own, `inst/tinytest/test-fit-cox.R`.

The integration test does not re-check what the unit
tests already cover. Instead it checks the seams: that
the output of `clean_cohort` is a valid input to
`fit_model`, and that the model summary has the
expected shape. A pipeline that passes its unit tests can
still fail here, if a column is renamed in one step
and read under its old name in the next.

### Data-validation tests

The third kind of test turns its attention from the
code to the data. Much of what goes wrong in a
health analysis is not a coding error but a data
defect. Examples are an age of two hundred, a
negative laboratory value, a treatment label
misspelled, or a column silently dropped by an
upstream export. A
data-validation test encodes the analyst's domain
knowledge as executable constraints and fails when
the data violates them.

Before writing constraints, we look first at what
we are constraining. @tbl-diabetic-arms tabulates
the retinopathy trial introduced in the conventions.
It is included here for a reason beyond
illustration: every cell in it can be counted
by hand from the data, which is precisely the
property an oracle needs. A test asserting that the
untreated arm contains
197 eyes, written as
that literal number, is checkable by
someone who does not trust the function that
produced it. A test asserting that it contains
`nrow(subset(d, trt == 0))` eyes is not a test at
all; it is the function agreeing with itself.


::: {#tbl-diabetic-arms .cell tbl-cap='Eyes and events by treatment arm in the diabetic retinopathy trial (`survival::diabetic`), the real dataset this book computes on. Each count is verifiable by hand from the 394 records, which is what makes the table usable as a test oracle rather than merely as a description.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tibble)
library(knitr)

d <- survival::diabetic
d$arm <- factor(d$trt, levels = c(0, 1),
                labels = c('Untreated', 'Laser'))

arms <- tibble(
  Arm = levels(d$arm),
  Eyes = as.integer(table(d$arm)),
  Events = as.integer(tapply(d$status, d$arm, sum)),
  `Event rate` = sprintf(
    '%.3f', as.numeric(tapply(d$status, d$arm, mean))
  )
)

kable(arms, align = 'lrrr')
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|Arm       | Eyes| Events| Event rate|
|:---------|----:|------:|----------:|
|Untreated |  197|    101|      0.513|
|Laser     |  197|     54|      0.274|


:::
:::


The difference between the arms is large and in the
expected direction. That is a reason to be careful
rather than pleased, because a validation test should
assert what the protocol requires, not what this
particular extract happens to show. An assertion that
the event rate in the laser arm is below one third
would pass today. It would fail on a different trial,
or on a corrected export, for reasons having nothing
to do with a defect.

```r
# abridged from inst/tinytest/test-cohort.R
raw <- load_cohort('../../analysis/data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv')
cohort <- clean_cohort(raw)

# the expected columns are present
expect_true(all(c('mrn', 'age_at_enroll', 'sex', 'incident_dm')
                %in% names(raw)))

# ages lie within the enrollment criteria, not merely
# within the observed range
expect_true(all(cohort$age_at_enroll >= 18 &
                cohort$age_at_enroll <= 105, na.rm = TRUE))

# sex takes only its two coded levels once cleaned
expect_true(all(cohort$sex %in% c('F', 'M')))

# outcome missingness stays within what the analysis
# can tolerate
expect_true(mean(is.na(cohort$incident_dm)) < 0.15)
```

These are the tests that most directly repay a
health scientist, because they catch the errors that
no amount of correct code can prevent, the errors
that live in the data before the analysis begins. In
a data-analysis or simulation archetype, where there
may be few reusable functions to unit-test, the
data-validation tests often carry most of the suite's
weight.

### Reproducibility tests

The fourth kind closes the loop back to the ladder.
A reproducibility test checks that a recorded result
regenerates. Its most tempting form runs a seeded
procedure twice in one session and asserts that the
two results agree:

```r
# a same-session check: it cannot detect what it
# appears to guard against
expect_equal(bootstrap_ci(cohort, B = 2000, seed = 2024),
             bootstrap_ci(cohort, B = 2000, seed = 2024))
```

Note first where the seed lives. `bootstrap_ci()` takes
it as an argument and sets it internally, with
`withr::with_seed()`, which also restores the caller's
generator state on exit. As a result, the function is
deterministic given its arguments and does not disturb
any random stream around it. A procedure that depends
on the caller setting a seed first is one `set.seed`
away from irreproducible, and moving the seed into the
signature makes forgetting it impossible.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall

A same-session check cannot fail for the reason it
seems to serve. Both calls run in the same R, under the
same random-number defaults, with the same package
versions. When an upgrade changes how `sample()` draws,
as R 3.6.0 did, both calls change together and still
agree. What the check does catch is narrower: a
procedure that ignores its seed. That is worth one line
in a unit test, but it is not a reproducibility test.
:::

A reproducibility test that can fail compares today's
result with one recorded in an earlier session and
committed to the repository. We call it a *baseline
test*. It has three parts: a script, run once, that
records the baseline; the committed baseline file; and
a test file that recomputes the quantities and compares
them with a stated tolerance.

```r
# analysis/scripts/generate_baseline.R, abridged. Run once
# from the project root to record the baseline, then commit
# inst/baseline/cohort_baseline.rds.
# The book's own baseline was recorded this way, and the
# file is now committed at that path; regenerate it only
# if the generator, the seed, or the model change.
result <- run_canonical_analysis(
  'analysis/data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv'
)
dir.create('inst/baseline', recursive = TRUE,
           showWarnings = FALSE)
saveRDS(result, 'inst/baseline/cohort_baseline.rds')
```

```r
# inst/tinytest/test-baseline-cohort.R, abridged: the
# real file also searches fallback paths for both files
raw_path <- '../../analysis/data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv'
if (!file.exists(raw_path)) {
  exit_file('raw extract absent; run simulate_cohort.R')
}
baseline <- readRDS(
  system.file('baseline', 'cohort_baseline.rds',
              package = 'reproducibility'))
result <- run_canonical_analysis(raw_path)

expect_equal(result$n_rows, baseline$n_rows,
  info = 'cleaned row count matches baseline')
expect_equal(result$n_events, baseline$n_events,
  info = 'event count matches baseline')
expect_equal(result$hr, baseline$hr, tolerance = 1e-8,
  info = 'Cox HR matches committed baseline')
expect_equal(result$lower, baseline$lower,
  tolerance = 1e-8,
  info = 'lower CI bound matches committed baseline')
expect_equal(result$upper, baseline$upper,
  tolerance = 1e-8,
  info = 'upper CI bound matches committed baseline')
```

Three details carry the weight. The path is relative
to `inst/tinytest/`, where `tinytest` runs the file. The
guard lets the file exit early under `R CMD check`,
which installs the package without `analysis/`. The
mirror in `inst/testdata/` covers the unit and
data-validation tests; the baseline test requires the
raw extract and skips cleanly without it. Finally, the
tolerance is stated and chosen, not left at a default.
`1e-8` relative is wide enough to absorb floating-point
summation reordered by a different BLAS or thread count
(@sec-containers), and far too narrow for a change in
the fitted coefficients to pass. A comparison with no
tolerance would fail on that reordering, and a check
that fails for reasons unrelated to the analysis trains
its reader to ignore it.

The test can be watched failing for the reason it
exists. The chunk below plays both sessions on the
synthetic cohort. It records the 97.5 percent bootstrap
bound for mean BMI under the sampler R used before
version 3.6.0 (`sample.kind = 'Rounding'`), as an
analysis recorded on an older R would have. It then
reruns it with the same seed and sampler, and reruns it
again with the same seed under the current default
(`'Rejection'`). The
comparison is the one `expect_equal()` makes, `all.equal()`
at the stated tolerance. `withr::with_seed()` sets the
sampler only for the duration of each call, and the final
`stopifnot()` confirms the session's generator is as it
was.


::: {#tbl-baseline-rng .cell tbl-cap='A baseline test across sessions. The bound recorded under the pre-3.6.0 sampler is reproduced exactly by a rerun with the same seed and sampler, and is not reproduced seed-exactly by a rerun with the same seed under the current default sampler, so the comparison at tolerance 1e-8 passes once and fails once. A same-session check would have passed in both cases.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(knitr)

cohort <- read.csv('../data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv')
bmi <- cohort$bmi[!is.na(cohort$bmi)]

boot_upper <- function(x, seed, sample_kind, reps = 2000) {
  withr::with_seed(
    seed,
    {
      means <- replicate(reps, mean(sample(x, replace = TRUE)))
      unname(quantile(means, 0.975))
    },
    .rng_sample_kind = sample_kind
  )
}

kind_before <- RNGkind()[3]

# R warns whenever the pre-3.6.0 sampler is selected;
# the warning is expected here and muffled.
baseline <- suppressWarnings(boot_upper(bmi, 2024, 'Rounding'))
rerun_same <- suppressWarnings(boot_upper(bmi, 2024, 'Rounding'))
rerun_new <- boot_upper(bmi, 2024, 'Rejection')

tol <- 1e-8
passes <- function(current) {
  isTRUE(all.equal(current, baseline, tolerance = tol))
}

checks <- data.frame(
  run = c('recorded baseline (Rounding)',
          'rerun, same seed and sampler (Rounding)',
          'rerun, same seed, current default (Rejection)'),
  upper_bound = c(baseline, rerun_same, rerun_new),
  passes = c('(baseline)',
             ifelse(passes(rerun_same), 'yes', 'no'),
             ifelse(passes(rerun_new), 'yes', 'no'))
)

stopifnot(identical(RNGkind()[3], kind_before))

kable(checks, digits = 4,
      col.names = c('Run', '97.5% bootstrap bound',
                    'Passes at tolerance 1e-8'))
```

|:---------------------------------------------|---------------------:|:------------------------|
|recorded baseline (Rounding)                  |               29.1400|(baseline)               |
|rerun, same seed and sampler (Rounding)       |               29.1400|yes                      |
|rerun, same seed, current default (Rejection) |               29.1436|no                       |


:::

The rerun under the current sampler moves the bound by
0.0036 units of
BMI, from 29.1400 to
29.1436. That is a small number,
and it is not a numerical artifact: the resamples
themselves are different. The baseline test reports it;
two calls in one session, both under whichever sampler
the session uses, would have agreed with each other and
reported nothing.

Failing the seed-exact comparison is not the same as
failing to reproduce the result, because the bound is
itself a Monte Carlo estimate. The chunk below estimates
its Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE) as the standard
deviation of the bound over 40 seeds, at the table's 2000
replicates, and then applies a two-tier check to the two
reruns.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mc_bounds <- vapply(1:40, function(s) boot_upper(bmi, s, 'Rejection'),
                    numeric(1))
mcse <- sd(mc_bounds)
two_tier <- compare_to_baseline(c(rerun_same, rerun_new),
                                c(baseline, baseline), mcse = mcse)
two_tier
#> [1] "exact"                    "within Monte Carlo error"

# Decimals an MCSE supports: the MCSE must be below half a
# unit of the last reported digit.
digits_supported <- function(mcse) max(0, floor(-log10(2 * mcse)))
d_bmi <- digits_supported(mcse)
# An MCSE from 40 seeds is itself uncertain by about 11
# percent, so two significant figures are all it supports.
sig2 <- function(x) {
  formatC(signif(x, 2), digits = 2, format = 'fg', flag = '#')
}
stopifnot(round(baseline, d_bmi) == round(rerun_new, d_bmi))
```
:::


The MCSE of the bound is 0.015, so the sampler
change is about
0.2 of
one MCSE. The seed-exact comparison fails, yet the change
is a fraction of one MCSE, and the statistical result
reproduces.

This is the two-tier baseline check. The first tier
compares at the numerical tolerance `1e-8`; a pass means
the draws themselves regenerated. On a failure, the second
tier accepts a difference of at most three MCSE, with the
MCSE recorded beside the baseline value.
`compare_to_baseline()` in the book's package implements
both tiers, and it returns 'exact' for the
same-sampler rerun and 'within Monte Carlo error' for the current
sampler. Both the recorded value and the rerun carry
Monte Carlo error, so their difference has a standard
deviation of about $\sqrt{2}$ MCSE. Under normality, three
MCSE then flags a pure change of draws about
3.4 percent of
the time, which is the price of a second tier that still
catches a real change.

The second tier applies only to a quantity that has
Monte Carlo error, such as a bootstrap bound or a
simulation summary. The Cox hazard ratio and its
confidence limits in `test-baseline-cohort.R` are
deterministic functions of the data, so only the first
tier applies to them, and `compare_to_baseline()` with
`mcse = NULL` reduces to it. The precision of the table
follows the same distinction. Its four decimals are there
for the seed-exact tier. As a statistical result, an MCSE
of 0.015 supports reporting the bound
as 29.1 under
either sampler, by the rule the next section gives.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}

To see this hold on your own machine: generate the raw

`sample.kind = 'Rejection'` against a baseline recorded
under `'Rounding'`, is this exact failure, executed in

:::

A baseline test is what L3 requires. The top rung, as
@sec-levels defines it, asks that recorded outputs be
shown to regenerate within a stated tolerance from a
clean rebuild. The baseline test supplies the recorded
outputs and the tolerance; running it inside an
environment rebuilt from its recipe supplies the clean
rebuild, and @sec-verification assembles the two in
continuous integration. A suite with no baseline test
can show that the code runs and that its functions are
correct on known inputs. However, it cannot show that
a recorded result regenerates, so it does not reach L3
however thorough it is. In the zzcollab composition,
`zzc verify --full` applies this rule. It stamps L3 only
when the image rebuilds, the test suite passes, and at
least one `inst/tinytest/test-baseline*.R` file exists
and is named in the test log. Otherwise it reports the
project as rebuilt and tested, at L2, with no baseline
comparison. A baseline whose guard exits early is still
named in the log, so the guard must not fire in the image.

## Monte Carlo error and parallel streams

@tbl-baseline-rng fixed the seed and varied only the
sampler (the default that R changed in version 3.6.0),
which isolated one source of change in the bootstrap
bound. A second source is always present and has nothing
to do with R versions. A bootstrap estimate is itself a
Monte Carlo quantity, built from a finite number of
resamples. It carries its own sampling variability on
top of the statistical sampling variability of the
original cohort. Two bootstrap runs at different seeds,
same data, same number of replicates `B`, will not return
exactly the same bound. The standard deviation of the
bound across seeds is its Monte Carlo standard error
(MCSE), distinct from the standard error the bootstrap is
estimating.

But how much does such a bound move in practice? The
practical diagnostic needs no extra theory: rerun the
same call at many seeds for a given `B`, and take the
standard deviation of the result; then raise `B` and watch
it shrink. The chunk below does this with `bootstrap_ci()`
on the HbA1c odds ratio, at `B = 250` and at the
package default `B = 1000`, with 20 seeds each.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cohort <- clean_cohort(
  load_cohort('../../analysis/data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv')
)
bounds_at <- function(B) {
  t(vapply(1:20, function(s) bootstrap_ci(cohort, B = B, seed = s),
           numeric(2)))
}
b250 <- bounds_at(250)
b1000 <- bounds_at(1000)
mcse250 <- apply(b250, 2, sd)
mcse1000 <- apply(b1000, 2, sd)
ratio <- mcse250 / mcse1000
# With 20 seeds the log of a ratio of two SDs has a standard
# error near sqrt(2 / 38); the prose calls the ratios
# consistent with 2 only while they are within two of them.
stopifnot(all(abs(log(ratio / 2)) < 2 * sqrt(2 / 38)))
d_upper <- digits_supported(mcse1000['upper'])
d_lower <- digits_supported(mcse1000['lower'])
stopifnot(d_upper < 2)
ci_default <- bootstrap_ci(cohort)
# Replicates for the MCSE to fall below half a unit of one
# more decimal, scaling the observed MCSE by 1/sqrt(B).
B_for <- function(mcse, d, B = 1000) {
  ceiling(B * (mcse / (0.5 * 10^-d))^2)
}
B_upper_next <- B_for(mcse1000['upper'], d_upper + 1)
```
:::


At `B = 250` the MCSE of the upper bound is
0.43 and that of the lower bound is
0.072. At `B = 1000` they are
0.22 and
0.040, on bounds near
5.5 and
1.5. An MCSE that
scales as $1/\sqrt{B}$ halves when `B` is quadrupled, and
the observed ratios are
2.0 for the upper bound and
1.8 for the lower. With 20
seeds, each estimated standard deviation is itself
uncertain by about
16 percent, so these ratios are
consistent with that scaling but do not pin it closely.

The standard guidance for simulation studies is to report
the MCSE of every Monte Carlo estimate and to choose the
number of repetitions from the precision required
[@morris2019]. Applied to reported digits, it gives a
rule for the number of replicates. Choose `B` so that the
MCSE of each reported quantity is below about half a unit
of its last reported digit, or report only the digits the
MCSE supports. At the default `B = 1000` the rule allows the
lower bound 1 decimal place and the upper bound
0, so the default call's interval should be
reported as
1.5
to
5.
Reporting the upper bound to one more decimal would need
about 19,000
replicates. A two-decimal interval from `bootstrap_ci()`
at its default therefore prints digits that are Monte
Carlo noise. The baseline test's `1e-8` in
@tbl-baseline-rng is a
numerical tolerance for one fixed sequence of draws, and
it says nothing about this. The MCSE is estimated once,
when choosing `B`, and recorded with the baseline as the
scale of the second tier; the test suite does not
re-estimate it on every run.

Resampling at the `B` a real analysis needs is often
parallelized across cores, and the random streams then
need as much care as the seed. Naive parallelization fails
first by irreproducibility. Under the default
Mersenne-Twister generator and the default
`mc.set.seed = TRUE`, `parallel::mclapply()` discards the
inherited generator state in each child process, which
then seeds itself from the clock and its process id. A
`set.seed()` before the call therefore does not fix the
result, and two runs differ. With `mc.set.seed = FALSE`
the children inherit the parent's state, and the workers
draw identical streams, so supposedly independent
replicates are duplicated. The L'Ecuyer-CMRG generator,
which `RNGkind('L\'Ecuyer-CMRG')` selects, was built to
provide many independent streams. Under it, `mclapply()`
gives each child its own stream, and
`parallel::clusterSetRNGStream()` gives one to each worker
of a cluster. Per-worker streams are independent, but the
result still depends on the number of workers. The
replicates are divided among the workers in chunks, so a
given replicate draws from a different stream when the
worker count changes.

Invariance to the worker count needs per-task streams: one
stream for each replicate, fixed before any worker starts.
`parallel::nextRNGStream()` can precompute them, the
`future.apply` package does so with `future.seed = TRUE`,
and the `doRNG` package does so for a `foreach` loop. The
book's package provides `replicate_streams()`, which
precomputes the streams with `nextRNGStream()` and runs
the replicates with `mclapply()`. The chunk below runs the
same 2000 bootstrap means of BMI on one worker and on two.
Forking is unavailable on Windows, where both runs are
sequential and the comparison is trivially true.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
boot_mean <- function(i) mean(sample(bmi, replace = TRUE))
one_worker <- replicate_streams(2000, boot_mean, seed = 2024,
                                cores = 1)
two_workers <- replicate_streams(2000, boot_mean, seed = 2024,
                                 cores = 2)
identical(one_worker, two_workers)
#> [1] TRUE
```
:::


The two runs are identical
(TRUE), replicate by
replicate, because replicate `i` draws from stream `i`
wherever it runs. The same seed discipline that makes a
serial bootstrap reproducible extends to a parallel one
only in this per-task form.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: two kinds of instability

A bootstrap bound changes when rerun with a different
seed at the same `B`. It also changes when rerun with the
same seed after an R version upgrade changes the default
sampler (@tbl-baseline-rng). Are these the same problem,
and does increasing `B` fix both?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

In size, largely yes; for the seed-exact check, no. The
seed-to-seed change at fixed `B` is Monte Carlo error, and
raising `B` shrinks it as $1/\sqrt{B}$. A new sampler
gives a given seed different resamples, which in effect
draws the bound at a new seed, so raising `B`
shrinks that change at the same rate. The two samplers
still disagree in the last digits at any `B`, so the
seed-exact tier keeps failing. Pinning the sampler
restores seed-exact agreement; the second tier, within
three MCSE, confirms that the statistical result
reproduced without it.
:::
:::

## Test behavior, not implementation

A test is worth writing only if it survives changes
that ought not to break it and fails on changes that
ought to. The way to secure this is to test what a
function does, its observable behavior, rather than
how it does it, its internal implementation. The
distinction is easiest to see in a pair of tests for
the same function:

```r
# fragile: pins an implementation detail
expect_true('filter' %in% all.names(body(my_clean)))

# robust: pins the behavior
result <- my_clean(data.frame(x = c(1, NA, 3)))
expect_false(anyNA(result))
```

The first test asserts that `my_clean` uses a
function called `filter` internally. If the analyst
later rewrites `my_clean` in base R, removing the
`filter` call while leaving its behavior
unchanged, the first test fails. It fails for no
good reason: the function still does exactly what it
promised. Such a test punishes honest refactoring
and trains the analyst to distrust the suite. The
second test asserts only that the cleaned data
carries no missing values, which is the behavior
that actually matters. It passes under any correct
implementation. As a general rule, a test should
fail when, and only when, the function's contract is
broken. Tests that fail for other reasons are a tax
on maintenance. Wilson and colleagues, in their
best-practices and
good-enough-practices guidance, make behavioral
testing a recurring recommendation [@wilson2014;
@wilson2017].

A corollary concerns how much to test. A test that
merely confirms a result is a data frame, without
checking any value in it, tests too little and gives
false comfort. A test that pins every incidental
property tests too much and breaks on every
revision. Deciding what to pin is the second of the
analyst's contributions named above, and no tool
makes that decision.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}

## Answer

It is an implementation test: it pins a detail of how

behavior but removes or renames that counter breaks
the test for no good reason, training the analyst to
distrust or delete it.
:::
:::

## Code quality as a validation feature

Testing confirms that code is correct. A second
family of tools confirms that code is *legible and
consistent*. Although these tools do not check
correctness directly, they belong to the same
validation register and serve the same
reproducibility end. The argument is one of
mechanism. Code that a reader can follow is code
whose errors a reader can find. Consistent
formatting removes the visual noise that hides a
transposed argument or a misplaced parenthesis.
Moreover, a single house style across a compendium
means that a difference in the code is always a
difference in meaning, never merely a difference in
whitespace. Wilson and colleagues, in both of their
practice papers, treat readable, conventional code
as a component of reproducible work rather than an
aesthetic preference [@wilson2014; @wilson2017].
Sandve and colleagues, in their ten simple rules,
make the companion point that the provenance and the
recorded results of an analysis must themselves be
preserved [@sandve2013].

Two tools mechanize this, and a third enforces them.

**Linting** is static analysis: `lintr` reads the
source without running it and flags stylistic
deviations and likely errors. Examples are an
assignment with `=` where the house style is `<-`, a
line past the width limit, a variable assigned and
never used, and a call to a function that does not
exist. Because it
does not execute the code, it catches a class of
mistake that tests, which only exercise the paths
they call, may miss.

**Styling** is automatic reformatting: `styler`
rewrites the source into a consistent layout,
fixing indentation, spacing, and alignment, so that
formatting is never a matter for human attention or
for a code review. The two are complementary;
`styler` fixes the formatting that `lintr` would
otherwise complain about.

In the framework, both run inside the project
container through Makefile targets, so that no host
R installation is required and every collaborator
runs the identical checks:

```bash
$ make style   # reformat R code with styler
$ make lint    # analyze R code with lintr
```

**A pre-commit hook** enforces them. A hook is a
script that git runs automatically at a defined
moment; a pre-commit hook runs before a commit is
recorded, and can refuse the commit if a check
fails. Configuring the linter and styler as a
pre-commit hook means that unstyled or unlinted code
cannot be committed from a clone where the hook is
installed, unless the analyst bypasses it with
`git commit --no-verify`. That is a stronger guarantee
than a convention that relies on memory, but a clone does
not carry the hook with it. The configuration
lives in a `.pre-commit-config.yaml` file at the
project root:

```yaml
# .pre-commit-config.yaml
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/lorenzwalthert/precommit
    rev: v0.4.3
    hooks:
      - id: style-files
      - id: lintr
      - id: readme-rmd-rendered
      - id: no-browser-statement
```

With this in place, an attempt to commit code that
`styler` would reformat, or that `lintr` flags, or
that contains a stray `browser()` left over from
debugging, is stopped before the commit completes.
The analyst is then prompted to fix it. The hook is
the fast local gate. A collaborator who has not
installed it is caught only if continuous integration
(@sec-verification) runs the same checks on the
server. The workflows in that chapter do not, so a
project that relies on the hook should add a step
running `lintr::lint_dir()` there.

## Check your understanding: capture or validation?

Classify each of the following as belonging to the
capture register or the validation register, and
say what would be lost by removing it. (a) The
`renv.lock` lockfile. (b) A unit test of
`calculate_mean`. (c) The `.pre-commit-config.yaml`
hook. (d) The Dockerfile.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

(a) Capture: it fixes the package
versions; removing it drops the analysis from L1 to
L0. (b) Validation: it checks that a captured
function is correct; removing it leaves the analysis
at the same level but now trusted rather than
checked. (c) Validation: it checks that code is
consistently formatted; removing it captures nothing
less but permits legibility to decay. (d) Capture:
it fixes the environment; removing it drops the
analysis from L2 to L1. The rule of thumb is that
removing a capture feature lowers the level, while
removing a validation feature leaves the level
unchanged and only stops the checking. There is one
exception: the baseline test is the evidence L3
requires, so removing it drops an analysis from L3 to
L2.
:::
:::

## Validation in the regulated sense

Every use of 'validation' in this chapter has been the
statistical and software-engineering sense: checking that
code is correct, that data meet a constraint, that a
result regenerates. In pharmaceutical, medical-device, and
other FDA- or EMA-regulated work, 'validation' names a
broader and more procedural idea. @sec-levels's warning
box introduces the distinction; this section develops the
three practices that fill it out for testing
specifically.

**Computer system validation.** Under 21 CFR 11.10(a),
a closed system that creates, modifies, maintains, or
transmits regulated electronic records must be validated
'to ensure accuracy, reliability, consistent intended
performance, and the ability to discern invalid or
altered records' [@cfr21part11]. The European Medicines
Agency sets parallel expectations for computerized
systems in clinical trials, and names statistical
software among them [@ema2023computerised]. This is
validation of the system
across its lifecycle, documented once and maintained by a
change-control process, not a one-time test run. The
regulation does not say how that validation is shown.
Installation, operational, and performance qualification
(IQ, OQ, and PQ) come from qualification practice, in
which a system qualification typically executes all
three [@nicholls2020], not from the text of 11.10. The
requirement's reach is also narrower than its wording
suggests. FDA's 2003 guidance on the scope and
application of Part 11 states that the agency will
exercise enforcement discretion over the Part 11
validation requirement, while the predicate rules, the
underlying requirements of the Act and of FDA's other
regulations, still apply, their own validation
requirements included [@fdapart11scope2003]. The R
Validation Hub concludes
that Part 11 is not relevant or mandatory for
statistical analysis software itself, though elements of
it apply when R is used as part of a validated system
[@nicholls2020]. What an inspector asks in practice is
whether the statistical computing environment is in a
documented, validated state under the sponsor's standard
operating procedures and the predicate rules. A
`tinytest` suite that passes is evidence toward that
state. It is not, by itself, that state, which also
rests on qualification records and a record of who
approved each change and when.

**Double programming.** Independent of any code-based
test, a regulated submission is commonly checked by
*double programming*. Two analysts, or one analyst and an
independent reviewer, implement the same analysis
separately, from the same specification, usually in
isolation from each other's code. The two results are
then compared. This is a different reproducibility
practice from everything else in this chapter. A baseline
test reruns the *same* code and checks that it still
returns the same answer; double programming runs *two
different* implementations of the same specification and
checks that they agree. Consider a bug shared by both
implementations, because both analysts misread the same
ambiguous protocol sentence. It would pass a baseline
test (the code is unchanged) and would also pass double
programming (the two analysts made the same mistake).
What double programming catches is a bug particular to
one implementation, the error a single analyst's code
review is least likely to find in their own work.

**Package risk assessment.** Pinning package versions,
as @sec-dependencies teaches, fixes which code runs. It
says nothing about how much to trust that code. But how
is that trust to be judged? The R Validation Hub, an R
Consortium working group formed for exactly this
question, proposes a risk-based answer [@nicholls2020].
The first step is to classify each package as either
'intended for use' (called directly by the analysis) or
an unexamined dependency reached only through another
package. The second is, for each intended-for-use
package, to assess its purpose, maintenance practice,
community usage, and existing test coverage. The third
is to have a qualified reviewer record a documented risk
judgment. Higher risk earns additional targeted testing.
Base R and the recommended packages are treated as
minimal risk. For other widely used packages, such as
the tidyverse, the white paper says only that there is a
reasonable case to treat their maintainers as a trusted
resource, and leaves that decision to each organization.
Whatever the risk score, tests are still required for
the statistical modeling functions of an
intended-for-use package. The `riskmetric`
package operationalizes several of these metrics so the
assessment does not start from nothing. This is a
judgment about trustworthiness layered on top of the
pinning @sec-dependencies already does, not a replacement
for it.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}

A compendium has a committed `renv.lock`, a passing
`tinytest` suite, and a documented sign-off that
`dplyr` 1.1.4 has been risk-assessed as trusted. An
inspector asks whether the statistical computing

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

All three are real evidence, but none is computer
system validation by itself, and the three together are
not automatically enough either. The lockfile is
capture; the test suite is software validation in this
chapter's sense; the risk assessment is a package-level
trust judgment. A validated state is defined by the
sponsor's procedures and required by the predicate
rules, not by these artifacts. It concerns the
environment as a whole across its lifecycle, maintained
through a change-control process. Under qualification
practice that means installation, operational, and
performance qualification records, and sign-off on each
subsequent change; 11.10(a) itself names none of these.
It is not met by a snapshot alone of the code, the
tests, and one package's status at a single point in
time.
:::
:::

## Reviewing analysis code {#sec-code-review}

Double programming is costly, because it implements every
output it covers twice. Most analyses, regulated or not,
are checked instead by review: a second analyst reads a
proposed change, usually as a pull request
(@sec-version-control), and approves it before it merges.
The two practices find different errors. A reviewer reads
one implementation against the plan, and is well placed
to see a wrong exclusion, a covariate the plan does not
name, or a seed set in the wrong place. A reviewer is
poorly placed to see an arithmetic slip in code that
reads correctly, which is the error a second, independent
implementation exposes. The choice between them is
therefore a judgment about risk, made per output and
recorded. One defensible arrangement is to double-program
the outputs a decision rests on, such as the primary
estimate, and to review the rest.

A reviewer needs a short list rather than a general
impression. For a pull request that changes an analysis,
we suggest six questions.

1. Does every output the change affects, whether a table,
   a figure, or a number in the prose, trace to committed
   code, with no value typed by hand?
2. Are the inputs read only from the raw data, never from
   a hand-edited intermediate file or an object left in a
   session?
3. Are the exclusions and derived variables the ones the
   analysis plan states, with the same thresholds and the
   same handling of missing values?
4. Is each seed set at the call that uses it, in the
   analysis code, rather than in `.Rprofile` or nowhere?
5. Did the tests change alongside the code, and does the
   pull request say why? An expected value edited to match
   new output needs the oracle that justifies the edit.
6. Does the log of the render or the test run show
   warnings nobody expected? A clean log is one in which
   every warning has been read and then removed or
   explained.

The list draws on the book's gates, but it is not a gate.
It asks for the judgments that continuous integration
cannot make (@sec-verification): whether a threshold
matches the plan, and whether a changed test was changed
for a good reason. The approval on the pull request then
records who checked the change and when, the same kind
of record the validated state described above rests on.
Questions 3 and 5 take the longest, because answering
them means opening the plan and the test diff rather
than reading the code alone.

## Testing across the archetypes

The four kinds of test are the same in every compendium,
but their relative weight shifts with the archetype.
@tbl-archetype-weight in @sec-compendium is the
reference. We state the shift here so that a student who
has met testing only in the context of R packages does
not wrongly conclude that a data analysis has nothing to
test. Testing is native to the **R-package** archetype,
whose suite is dominated by unit tests that `R CMD check`
runs as a matter of course. The **data-analysis** and
**simulation** archetypes, by contrast, may have few
reusable functions and no exported interface. In these
the data-validation and reproducibility tests carry the
weight instead. A simulation in particular leans on a
baseline test that fixes the seed and compares the result
with a committed value, since its entire output is a
function of that seed. @sec-verification develops the
point at length. The **manuscript** archetype adds a test
that the report renders and that its headline numbers
match a baseline. The **blog** archetype tests the
functions and example computations its posts depend on.
That is a reproducibility obligation to readers no
smaller than a manuscript's to its reviewers.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}

must regenerate. Those are exactly what data-validation
and baseline tests check.

## Worked example

We now make the paradox concrete and executable. The
following chunk defines the `calculate_mean` function
in two forms, one correct and one carrying the bug of
the orientation, and checks each against three inputs
whose means are known by hand. Rather than call the
`tinytest` package, which may be absent from a bare R
session, we hand-roll a one-line expectation. That is
all a bare check really is: a comparison of an actual
value against an expected one.


::: {#tbl-paradox .cell tbl-cap='A correct function and a buggy variant checked against three inputs with hand-computed means. The buggy variant returns the same wrong value on every input and would return it on every machine and every rerun: it is perfectly reproducible and still wrong.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
# the function under test, in a correct and a
# buggy form
calculate_mean <- function(x, na.rm = FALSE) {
  if (na.rm) x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  sum(x) / length(x)
}

calculate_mean_buggy <- function(x) {
  sum(x)                 # bug: division dropped
}

# a minimal hand-rolled expectation: no testing
# package required
expect <- function(actual, expected, tol = 1e-8) {
  isTRUE(abs(actual - expected) < tol)
}

# three inputs whose means are known independently
cases <- list(c(1, 2, 3),
              c(10, 20, 30, 40),
              c(5, 5, 5, 5, 5))
oracle <- c(2, 25, 5)

results <- data.frame(
  input = vapply(cases,
                 function(x) paste(x, collapse = ', '),
                 character(1)),
  expected = oracle,
  correct = vapply(cases, calculate_mean, numeric(1)),
  buggy = vapply(cases, calculate_mean_buggy,
                 numeric(1))
)
results$correct_passes <-
  mapply(expect, results$correct, oracle)
results$buggy_passes <-
  mapply(expect, results$buggy, oracle)

knitr::kable(results)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|input          | expected| correct| buggy|correct_passes |buggy_passes |
|:--------------|--------:|-------:|-----:|:--------------|:------------|
|1, 2, 3        |        2|       2|     6|TRUE           |FALSE        |
|10, 20, 30, 40 |       25|      25|   100|TRUE           |FALSE        |
|5, 5, 5, 5, 5  |        5|       5|    25|TRUE           |FALSE        |


:::
:::


The correct function passes every check; the buggy
function fails every check, and it fails them
identically. Were we to rerun this chunk a thousand
times, on a thousand machines, the `buggy` column
would hold the same wrong values every time. The bug
is not a source of variability, which reproducibility
tooling might eventually surface. It produces the
same error on every run, and only a comparison
against an independent oracle can catch it. That
comparison is what a test is.

In a real compendium, the hand-rolled `expect` gives
way to the `tinytest` expectations, and the checks
live in a file under `inst/tinytest/`. The following
is that file, shown as a static listing that is not
run here. It is exactly the unit test that would have
caught the bug before it reached a result:

```r
# inst/tinytest/test-calculate_mean.R
expect_equal(calculate_mean(c(1, 2, 3)), 2)
expect_equal(calculate_mean(c(10, 20, 30, 40)), 25)
expect_equal(calculate_mean(rep(5, 5)), 5)
expect_true(is.nan(calculate_mean(numeric(0))))
expect_equal(calculate_mean(c(1, NA, 3),
                            na.rm = TRUE), 2)
```

The runner `tests/tinytest.R` that `R CMD check`
invokes is a three-line file:

```r
# tests/tinytest.R
if (requireNamespace('tinytest', quietly = TRUE)) {
  tinytest::test_package('mycompendium')
}
```

and the pre-commit configuration shown earlier
completes the picture. The linter and styler guard
the code's legibility on every commit, and the
tinytest suite guards its correctness. Continuous
integration re-runs both on a clean machine, so that
neither guarantee depends on the author's local
setup.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: the oracle in the table

In @tbl-paradox, why is `oracle <- c(2, 25, 5)` written
by hand in the chunk rather than computed by calling
`calculate_mean()` on the three `cases`?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Because an oracle has to come from outside the code
under test. Computing the expected values by calling
`calculate_mean()` would make the check compare the
function against itself. It would pass identically
whether `calculate_mean` were correct or carried the
dropped-division bug, since both forms are internally
consistent with their own output. The hand-written
vector is what lets the table show the buggy column
failing every row.
:::
:::

## Collaborating with an LLM

A language model is a capable assistant for writing
tests, and a dangerous one for a specific reason: it
can readily produce tests that pass, which is not
the same as tests that are correct. The analyst's
verification duty is heaviest exactly where the
model is most fluent.

::: {.callout-important}
## Restricted data

One rule comes first (habit 3). Never paste or upload
protected health information, identifiable records, or data
held under a data use agreement, nor outputs derived from
them, into a model or a coding agent unless three conditions
all hold. The institution has approved that endpoint for
that class of data. The IRB protocol and the consent permit
the processing. The data use agreement, or the provider's
terms, permits it. If any of the three is unclear, the
answer is no.

The third condition is the one most often missed.
Institutional approval of a tool does not override the terms
under which a data provider released the data. NIH, for
example, treats sharing controlled-access data through
prompts with public generative AI tools, which it glosses as
third-party tools, as a breach of the data use certification.
It treats a model trained on such data as a data derivative,
to be shared only with other approved users and not kept
after the project closes [@nihgenai2025].

Describe the structure instead: the column names and types,
or a small synthetic example generated from the data
dictionary, never edited from real rows. A coding agent sees
whatever files are in its working tree, so run it in a
checkout or container where the real data is not mounted.

An agent also acts, so confine it to a branch and keep merges,
pushes, and deposits for yourself (@sec-llm-delegate).
:::


Tests sit close to the data, so the derived outputs the
rule covers include a failing test's printout of
offending rows. The book's simulated cohort is a
suitable synthetic example to describe instead.

**Prompt.** 'Here is my `calculate_mean` function.
Write `tinytest` unit tests for it, including edge
cases.'

*Watch for.* Check whether each expected value was
derived by running the function it was given, rather
than by independent computation. If the function is
buggy, an oracle derived that way matches the bug,
producing tests that pass against wrong behavior and
thereby certifying the error. Check also for tests of
only the paths the code obviously takes, which miss
the empty vector or the missing value.

*Verification.* Check every expected value by hand
or from an independent formula, not by running the
function, since the oracle must come from outside the
code under test. Confirm that the edge cases you care
about, the empty input, the single value, the missing
value, each have a test.

**Prompt.** 'Here is the data dictionary, not the
data, for my cohort: `age_at_enroll` (integer, years),
`sex` (character, coded `F` or `M` after cleaning),
`bmi` (numeric, kg/m^2), `incident_dm` (integer, 0 or
1). Write `tinytest` data-validation tests for a data
frame with these columns.'

*Watch for.* Check for generic checks, such as
non-missing identifiers and numeric outcomes, that are
reasonable but do not encode *your* domain.
The dictionary gives types and codes. It does not give
the protocol's eligibility ages, the plausible range
of BMI in your population, or how much outcome
missingness the analysis can tolerate, so any such
bound in the answer was supplied by the model rather
than by your protocol.

*Verification.* Supply the domain constraints
yourself, or check that the generated ranges match
your data dictionary. A validation test asserting a
plausible-looking but wrong range is worse than no
test, because it lends false authority.

**Prompt.** 'Explain why this test is failing.'

*Watch for.* The model may recommend changing the
test to match the current output, which makes the
failure disappear without establishing whether the
code or the test was wrong. A failing test is
sometimes correct: it may be reporting a real bug.

*Verification.* Decide first, from the oracle,
whether the code or the expectation is at fault, and
only then change the one that is wrong. Never
silence a failing test by editing its expected value
to whatever the code currently returns; that
converts a test into a tautology.

*A better prompt.* 'The attached `tinytest` file
fails on the line shown, with this message. The
expected value was computed by hand from the analysis
plan. Do not edit the test file. List the possible
causes in the function, and for each give an input I
can run, with its hand-computed answer, that would
confirm or rule it out.'

A coding agent with write access need not stop at a
recommendation: asked to make the suite pass, it can
make the edit itself, and the change arrives as an
ordinary commit. Treat `inst/tinytest/` and
`inst/baseline/` as protected paths, and read every
line of any diff that touches them before it merges,
as question 5 of @sec-code-review asks. What an agent
may change and what stays with the analyst is set out
in @sec-llm-delegate.

## The cohort, continued {#sec-cohort-continued-testing}

The chapter has introduced four kinds of test. This
section applies all four to the running cohort
compendium, using the canonical Cox analysis as the
analysis under test.

**The canonical analysis.** The primary question is:
does BMI predict time to incident diabetes after
adjusting for age and sex? The model is a Cox
proportional-hazards model fit to the cleaned extract,
with BMI expressed per 5 kg/m^2 so that the hazard
ratio has a clinically natural scale. The analysis
runs clean only after `clean_cohort()` has repaired
the four planted defects.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(survival)
cohort_path <- file.path(
  '..', '..', 'analysis', 'data', 'raw_data',
  'cohort_raw.csv')
raw    <- load_cohort(cohort_path)
cohort <- clean_cohort(raw)
fit    <- fit_cox(cohort)
res    <- summarise_cox(fit)
```
:::


The hazard ratio for BMI per 5 kg/m^2 is
1.83 (95% CI
1.32--2.52),
based on 48 events from
337 cleaned rows. Uncleaned, the analysis
would still run, but it would fit a different model to
the 338-row raw extract, with the duplicate
and the miscoded sex included.

**Unit tests of `fit_cox()`.** A unit test checks
the contract of one function in isolation. For
`fit_cox()` the contract is about which rows the model
uses. `coxph()` drops every row with a missing value on
any variable it reads, so the model uses the complete
cases on `followup_days`, `incident_dm`, `bmi`,
`age_at_enroll`, and `sex`, and its event count is the
number of events among those cases, not the number of
non-missing outcomes. The oracle is computed from the data
directly rather than from the fit, so a change to the
exclusion rule fails the test. The assertions below are in
`inst/tinytest/test-fit-cox.R`.

```r
model_vars <- c('followup_days', 'incident_dm', 'bmi',
                'age_at_enroll', 'sex')
complete <- stats::complete.cases(cohort[, model_vars])

expect_equal(fit$n, sum(complete),
  info = 'the model uses the complete cases on its variables')
expect_equal(fit$nevent,
             sum(cohort$incident_dm[complete] == 1),
  info = 'the event count is the events among complete cases')
expect_true(fit$nevent < sum(!is.na(cohort$incident_dm)),
  info = 'events are fewer than non-missing outcomes')
```

On the cleaned cohort the model uses 305 of the
337 rows, and its 48 events are
the rows among them with `incident_dm` equal to 1. A
count of non-missing outcomes, here
305, would count the
zeros as events too. The same file also removes the age of one event
row and checks that exactly one event and one row leave
the model.

**Integration test of the pipeline.** An integration
test checks that the pipeline stages compose
correctly end to end: `load_cohort` feeds
`clean_cohort` feeds `fit_cox` feeds `summarise_cox`,
and the final result is a list with the expected
names and no `NA` values. This listing and the two
after it are illustrative and abridged, and the book's
suite does not run them as written.

```r
result <- run_canonical_analysis(cohort_path)
expect_true(all(c('n_rows', 'hr', 'lower',
                   'upper', 'n_events')
                %in% names(result)),
  info = 'canonical result has expected names')
expect_true(all(!is.na(unlist(result))),
  info = 'canonical result contains no NA values')
```

**Data-validation tests.** The planted pathologies
give the data-validation suite something real to
catch. The test file checks each defect before and
after cleaning, so a change to `clean_cohort()` that
accidentally fixes or breaks a defect fails a test
instead of silently altering the baseline.

```r
# Duplicate before cleaning, gone after
expect_equal(sum(duplicated(raw$mrn)), 1,
  info = 'raw extract has exactly one duplicated MRN')
expect_equal(sum(duplicated(cohort$mrn)), 0,
  info = 'cleaned cohort has no duplicated MRN')

# Implausible age before cleaning
expect_true(any(raw$age_at_enroll > 105, na.rm = TRUE),
  info = 'raw extract has at least one implausible age')
expect_true(all(is.na(cohort$age_at_enroll) |
                cohort$age_at_enroll <= 105),
  info = 'cleaned cohort has no age above 105')
```

**Reproducibility (baseline) test.** The baseline
test is the L3 step. It reruns `run_canonical_analysis()`
and compares the hazard ratio and confidence limits
with values in `inst/baseline/cohort_baseline.rds`,
within a relative tolerance of `1e-8`.

```r
baseline <- readRDS(
  system.file('baseline', 'cohort_baseline.rds',
              package = 'reproducibility'))
result   <- run_canonical_analysis(cohort_path)

expect_equal(result$hr, baseline$hr,
  tolerance = 1e-8,
  info = 'Cox HR matches committed baseline')
expect_equal(result$lower, baseline$lower,
  tolerance = 1e-8,
  info = 'lower CI bound matches committed baseline')
```

A failure here means either the extract changed
(check `shasum -a 256 cohort_raw.csv`), the `survival`
package version changed (check `renv.lock`), the R
version changed (check `sessionInfo()`), or the
model specification changed (check the diff of
`R/cohort.R`). A baseline that also records a Monte
Carlo quantity, such as a bootstrap bound, has a fifth
cause: the random-number generator changed (check
`RNGkind()` against the recorded kind). The question
there is whether the difference is within Monte Carlo
error, which the second tier of `compare_to_baseline()`
answers. Each cause has a different fix; the baseline
test names the symptom and the diagnosis follows from the
audit.

## Exercise 1

The form of the answer matters more than the function
chosen. For a hypothetical `summarize_visits()`:

```r
# inst/tinytest/test-summarize_visits.R
expect_equal(summarize_visits(c(2, 4, 6)), 4)
expect_true(is.nan(summarize_visits(numeric(0))))
expect_error(summarize_visits('a'))
```

Where each expected value came from is the substance of
the exercise, and the three answers should be different.

The ordinary case comes from arithmetic done by hand,
independently of the function. This is what makes it an
oracle. If the expected value were computed by running the
function, the test would assert only that the function
agrees with itself, which is the commonest way a test
suite becomes worthless.

The empty-input case comes from a decision about the
contract. There is no arithmetic to do; the analyst must
decide what the function should do with no data and then
encode the decision. The test is as much a specification
as a check.

The wrong-type case comes from the same contract,
asserting that the function refuses input it cannot
handle rather than returning something misleading.

If you cannot state where an expected value came from,
you have usually written a change-detector rather than
a test.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 2

The bug is the dropped division, so the function returns a
sum where a mean is intended:

```r
summarize_visits <- function(x) sum(x)   # bug
```

The analysis still runs, produces a number, and produces
the *same* number on every machine and every rerun. If the
project is containerized and its packages pinned, that
number is perfectly reproducible.

The catching test is the ordinary case from exercise 1:

```r
expect_equal(summarize_visits(c(2, 4, 6)), 4)
```

It fails immediately, returning 12 against an expected 4.

**Why reproduction did not catch it.** Because reproduction
asks whether the same inputs give the same outputs, and
they do. The buggy function is deterministic; nothing about
it varies between machines or over time. Reproducibility
machinery captures determinants and propagates whatever
the code computes with mechanical fidelity, including the
wrong thing. The only way to detect the error is to compare
the output against a value obtained *independently of the
code*. That is what the hand-computed oracle supplies, and
what no amount of environment capture can.
:::
