## Exercise 4

**All of them belong to the validation register.** Unit
tests and data-validation tests alike pin no determinant:
they add no package to the lockfile and no library to the
image. They confirm that what was captured behaves as
intended.

**What removing them would change.** Nothing about the
position on the L0 to L3 ladder. An analysis at L2 with a
full test suite and the same analysis at L2 with no tests
sit on the same rung. The rung grades how far down the
determinant stack the result is locked, and tests lock
nothing.

**What removing them would change instead** is whether
anyone has reason to believe the result is right. The
analysis becomes trusted rather than checked, and the
class of error the tests were catching, a wrong function
and an out-of-range dataset, returns to being invisible.

One qualification concerns L3. L3 requires that
recorded outputs be shown to regenerate within a stated
tolerance from a clean rebuild, and the evidence for that
is a baseline test. The unit and data-validation tests of
exercises 1 and 3 are not baseline tests, so removing them
leaves L3 where it was. Removing the baseline test, by
contrast, would drop a project from L3 to L2, because the one piece of
evidence the rung requires would be gone. It is the
*verification role* that matters there, not the testing
role.
:::

## Exercise 5

```r
# once, from the project root, to record the baseline
cohort <- clean_cohort(
  load_cohort('analysis/data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv')
)
saveRDS(coef(fit_model(cohort)),
        'inst/tinytest/baseline-coefs.rds')
```

```r
# inst/tinytest/test-baseline-coefs.R
data_file <- '../../analysis/data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv'
if (!file.exists(data_file)) exit_file('no analysis data')
baseline <- readRDS('baseline-coefs.rds')
cohort <- clean_cohort(load_cohort(data_file))
current <- coef(fit_model(cohort))
expect_equal(current, baseline, tolerance = 1e-8,
             info = 'model coefficients match the baseline')
```

The model fit draws no random numbers, so no seed is
needed; a stochastic quantity would take its seed as an
argument, as `bootstrap_ci()` does in the chapter. The
file name begins `test-baseline`, the convention by which
a verification step finds baseline tests. Changing one
line of the analysis makes the test fail, reporting the
coefficients that moved.

The tolerance is the part of this exercise that needs
thought. An exact comparison is the strongest check,
and it will produce failures that mean nothing.
Floating-point summation reorders under a different BLAS
or a different thread count, as @sec-containers discusses,
and the last digits move without the analysis changing.
Two different tolerances are in play, and you should
name each. The *numerical* tolerance, `1e-8` relative
here, accepts that floating-point noise and still catches
any change in the fitted model large enough to alter a
reported figure. The *reporting* tolerance is the
precision at which results are published; for a Monte
Carlo quantity it is set by the MCSE, as the second tier
of the chapter's baseline check is. Because these
coefficients draw no random numbers, only the numerical
tolerance applies to them. A numerical tolerance set
loosely, near the reporting precision, stops detecting
real changes.

**What this test is and is not.** It is the kind of
baseline test L3 requires, and it is a *change detector*.
It asserts that today's answer matches the recorded one,
not that either is correct, because the baseline was
produced by the same code it now guards. If the code was
wrong when the baseline was recorded, this test will
faithfully defend the wrong answer. That is the paradox
reappearing one level up.
The unit tests of exercise 1 are what establish
correctness; this test establishes stability.
:::

## Exercise 6

**What the hook does.** The commit is refused. The
formatting hook rewrites the offending files in place and
aborts, so the commit does not complete and the working
tree now contains the reformatted code, which must be
staged and committed again. The effect is that
misformatted code cannot enter the history at all.

**The contrast with continuous integration.** CI would let
the commit through. The code enters the history, the push
succeeds, and the check runs afterward on the server,
reporting a failure against a commit that already exists.
Fixing it requires a second commit, so the history now
records both the violation and its repair.

The differences worth naming are three. **Timing:** the
hook acts before the record is written, CI after.
**Locality:** the hook runs on the analyst's machine and
can therefore be skipped, with `--no-verify` or by a
collaborator who never installed it, whereas CI runs on
the server and cannot. **Scope:** the hook must be fast
enough to sit inside a commit, so it does cheap things
like formatting and linting, whereas CI can rebuild the
container and run the full suite.

The two are complements rather than alternatives, and the
chapter's framing explains why. The hook is a convenience
that keeps trivia out of the history. CI is the gate that
actually guarantees anything, because it is the one nobody
can skip.
:::

## Exercise 8

The code must be committed first, then the recording
script is run against that committed code, and the
baseline file it writes is committed second, in its own
commit. This is habit 1 applied to a derived
artifact rather than to the primary analysis: a committed
file must always be traceable to the committed code that
produced it.

Reversing the order breaks that traceability. Suppose the
baseline is regenerated and committed while the code
change that motivated it is still uncommitted. A
collaborator who pulls the repository then receives the
new baseline paired with the *old* code, because the code
change never reached the shared history. Their copy of
the baseline test then fails immediately, not because
anything is wrong with their checkout, but because the
repository itself never recorded a consistent pair of
code and baseline. Worse, if the local, uncommitted code
change is later lost, the committed baseline becomes
orphaned. It is then a recorded result with no committed
code that anyone can point to as having produced it,
which is exactly the provenance gap habit 1 exists to
close.
:::

## Exercise 9

Your functions and findings will differ; the answer
takes the form of the review comments, the replies, and
the comparison. Four places in this plan repay a
reviewer's attention, because each is where your two
functions can diverge while both run without error.

**Ages.** The plan sets an implausible age to missing.
A function that drops the row instead changes the row
count, and the change appears only if you count rows
before and after. This is question 3.

**Missing outcomes.** The plan keeps rows whose outcome
is missing, because dropping them is an analytic
decision that the model step makes. A cleaning function
that drops them has moved that decision into the wrong
place.

**Duplicates.** 'One row per `mrn`' does not say which
copy to keep. Check whether the duplicated rows agree on
every column. If they do not, the plan is ambiguous, and
the fix belongs in the plan, recorded and dated, not in
whichever choice each of you happened to code.

**Coding and parsing.** Look at every distinct value of
`sex` and every format in `enroll_date` in the raw file
before deciding that the plan's rules cover them. A
value the rules do not name should become missing by a
stated rule, not by accident.

The comparison is double programming in miniature. Use
`all.equal()` on the two cleaned data frames, after
sorting both by `mrn`, and read every difference it
reports. Review is suited to the departures from the
plan that are visible in the code, such as a dropped
row; the comparison is suited to the slips that read
correctly, such as a date format parsed in the wrong
order. If the two functions agree, that is evidence
for both, but not proof: you may have read the same
sentence of the plan the same wrong way, as the section
on double programming warns.
:::

## Cheat sheet {#sec-cheat-testing}

| Command or rule | What it does |
|---|---|
| `expect_equal(a, e)` | Compares `a` to oracle `e` with `all.equal()`'s default tolerance. |
| `expect_equal(a, e, tolerance = 1e-8)` | The baseline-test comparison: a stated, not default, tolerance (habit 5). |
| `expect_true()`, `expect_false()`, `expect_identical()`, `expect_error()`, `expect_inherits()` | The common `tinytest` expectations beyond equality. |
| `tinytest::test_package('pkg')` | Runs the suite under `inst/tinytest/` via the `tests/tinytest.R` runner. |
| `exit_file('message')` | Exits a test file early, for a test that needs data `R CMD check` does not install. |
| `make lint` / `make style` | Run `lintr` / `styler` inside the project container. |
| `test-baseline*.R` naming | The convention `zzc verify --full` looks for to certify L3. |
| Rule of thumb | Test behavior, not implementation; a test should fail only when the contract breaks. |
| Rule of thumb | An oracle must be computed independently of the code under test, never by calling it. |
| Habit 4 | Make every gate able to fail, and watch it fail once. |
| Habit 5 | Compare against a recorded baseline, with a stated tolerance. |
| Code review, six questions (@sec-code-review) | Output traces to code; raw inputs; the plan's exclusions; seed at the call; tests changed with a reason; clean log |

## Further reading

The single most important reference for this chapter
is the short note by Leek and Peng, that reproducible
research can still be wrong [@leek2015]. It states the
paradox that motivates every test in a compendium, and
it argues for a prevention-oriented rather than a
correction-oriented stance toward analytical error.

For the testing tool itself, van der Loo's
documentation of `tinytest` [@vanderloo2020] explains
the design rationale for a zero-dependency,
bare-expectation framework. It is worth reading for
the argument that a testing framework should not
itself be a heavy dependency.

For the practice of testing and code quality as
components of scientific computing, the two papers by
Wilson and colleagues are the standard references.
They are the best-practices paper [@wilson2014] and the
good-enough-practices paper [@wilson2017], the latter
pitched deliberately at researchers without a
software background. Sandve and colleagues' ten
simple rules [@sandve2013] cover the same ground in a
compact, rule-by-rule form, and situate version control
and recorded results within a general reproducibility
discipline.

The connection between testing and the highest rung
of the ladder is taken up in @sec-verification, where
the reproducibility test of this chapter reappears at
the scale of the whole compendium as output
verification. @sec-levels gives the
capture-and-validation distinction that places testing
in the validation register. Peng's early account of
reproducibility as a spectrum [@peng2011] remains the
clearest short statement of why reproducibility can serve
as a minimum scientific standard when full independent
replication is not possible.
